Affiliation:: School of Computer Science, University of Oklahoma
Techniques Used: Theoretical derivation of upper and lower bound formulas
Synthetic thread generation with parameterized CPU usage factors
Data & Platforms: University of Oklahoma distributed system simulation environment
Application Areas: Dynamic Task Scheduling in Distributed Systems
Resource Availability Modeling for Concurrent Applications
Load Balancing and Process Assignment Optimization
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Composite Analytical Bounds Derivation: Formulating tight upper and lower bounds for execution efficiency by integrating CPU availability models with memory constraint analysis, validated against real-world benchmarks on UNIX systems to support robust scheduling decisions.

Heterogeneous Hardware Performance Modeling: Predicting GPU kernel execution efficiency by analyzing thread block and warp residency parameters on specific architectures (Tesla C1060, Kepler 20), achieving prediction errors between 0.13% and 5.69% to optimize thread arrangements.

Statistical CPU Availability Prediction: Deriving theoretical formulas for CPU availability of concurrent Java threads based on synthetic thread generation and empirical loading conditions, identifying high predictability under light/heavy loads versus moderate variability.

Biasing Strategy for Scheduling Robustness: Enhancing dynamic scheduling algorithms in distributed systems by implementing partial task completion feedback and resource requirement biasing (constant, proportionate) to counteract model underestimation and improve execution reliability.
Summary Description: John Antonio specializes in performance modeling and dynamic scheduling for multi-core and heterogeneous computing environments. His research focuses on deriving analytical bounds for CPU and memory availability to predict the execution efficiency of concurrent Java applications and GPU kernels. By combining theoretical derivations with empirical validation on platforms like NVIDIA CUDA and UNIX systems, he develops robust scheduling strategies that mitigate resource estimation errors. His work significantly advances load balancing, process assignment, and the reliability of distributed systems under uncertain resource conditions.
